First, notice that $F(x)$ is an even function. So, the Fourier series of its $2L$-periodic extension has the form

$$
\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{L}).

$$
f(x)∼3+\frac{7{\pi }^{2}}{6}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{14(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx).

- the function $F$ is continuously differentiable on $(-\pi ,\pi ),$

First, notice that $F(x)$ is an even function. So, the Fourier series of its $2L$-periodic extension has the form

$$
\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{L}).
$$

In our case, $L=2$ and we are already given the coefficients ${a}_{0}$ and ${a}_{n}$ for $n\ge 1.$ Thus, the Fourier series of $f(x)$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼-\frac{13}{3}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{64(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Now, notice that 

- the function $F$ is continuously differentiable on $(-2,2),$

- continuous on $[-2,2),$ and

- satisfies $F(-2)=F(2),$ if we extend the value at $x=2$ using the formula $F(x)=-4{x}^{2}+1.$

Therefore, the $4$-periodic extension $f$ is $\text{continuous}$ and $\text{piecewise smooth}$ on $R,$ so we may differentiate its Fourier series term-by-term:

q-343391.worked_solution:
First, notice that $F(x)$ is an even function. So, the Fourier series of its $2L$-periodic extension has the form

$$
\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{L}).
$$

In our case, $L=\pi $ and we are already given the coefficients for $n\ge 1.$ Thus, the Fourier series of $f(x)$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼{\pi }^{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{12(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx).
$$

Now, notice that the function $F$ is continuous on $(-\pi ,\pi ).$ 
Therefore, the $2\pi $-periodic extension $f$ is $\text{piecewise continuous}$ on $R,$ so we may integrate its Fourier series term-by-term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{x}3{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t & ∼{\int }_{0}^{x}({\pi }^{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{12(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nt))\text{d}t \\ [{t}^{3}]_{0}^{x} & ∼[{\pi }^{2}t]_{0}^{x}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{12(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}}\cdot [\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nt)]_{0}^{x} \\ {x}^{3} & ∼{\pi }^{2}x+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{12(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}

Let $f(x)$ be the $4$-periodic extension of the function $F(x)=8x$ defined on $[-2,2).$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below, showing the derivation of a series converging to the $4$-periodic extension of 

$$

$$

from the corresponding Fourier series of $f(x).$The Fourier series of $f(x)$ is given by

q-342023.worked_solution:
First, notice that $F(x)$ is an odd function. So, the Fourier series of its $2L$-periodic extension has the form

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{L}).
$$

In our case, $L=2$ and we are already given the coefficients ${b}_{n}$ for $n\ge 1.$ Thus, the Fourier series of $f(x)$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{32(-1)^{n+1}}{n\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Now, notice that the function $F$ is continuous on $(-2,2).$ 
Therefore, the $4$-periodic extension $f$ is $\text{piecewise continuous}$ on $R,$ so we may integrate its Fourier series term-by-term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{x}8t\,\text{d}t & ∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{32(-1)^{n+1}}{n\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi t}{2})\,\text{d}t \\ [4{t}^{2}]_{0}^{x} & ∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{32(-1)^{n+1}}{n\pi }\cdot [-\frac{2}{n\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi t}{2})]_{0}^{x} \\ 4{x}^{2} & ∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{64(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}\cdot (1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}))\end{aligned}
$$
